nameStory: The Alpine Bloodspot Lichen gets its dramatic name from the dark reddish-brown spots that dot its surface, looking like tiny drops of blood against pale rock. The "alpine" part refers to its preference for high elevation, windswept locations where few other organisms can survive.
description: Alpine Bloodspot Lichen is a crusty, flat lichen that forms irregular patches on rocks in New England's highest peaks. It creates a thin, pale grayish or whitish crust dotted with distinctive dark reddish-brown to blackish spots that give it its "bloodspot" name. These patches can spread several inches across, hugging tightly to the rock surface like a living paint job that's been splattered with dark drops.

idTips.label: Dark red-brown spots
idTips.description: Look for distinctive dark reddish-brown to nearly black circular spots scattered across the pale surface, resembling dried blood drops on stone

idTips.label: Crusty texture
idTips.description: Feels rough and granular to the touch, forming a thin but firmly attached crust that you can't peel off the rock

idTips.label: Pale background color
idTips.description: The main body appears whitish to pale gray, creating strong contrast with the dark spots

idTips.label: Rock-hugging growth
idTips.description: Grows as irregular patches that follow the contours of the rock surface, never forming leafy or shrubby structures

idTips.label: High elevation preference
idTips.description: Most commonly found on exposed rocks above treeline or on mountain summits where wind and weather are harsh

habitat: Alpine Bloodspot Lichen thrives on exposed rocky surfaces at high elevations throughout New England's mountains, particularly above treeline on peaks like Mount Washington and other summits in the White Mountains. It prefers bare rock faces, boulders, and cliff surfaces that receive full sun and are regularly scoured by wind and weather.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more visible as snow melts away from high elevation rocks, revealing patches that survived winter's harsh conditions. The contrast between spots and background may be most pronounced now.
seasonality.summer: Most accessible to observers during hiking season when mountain trails are clear. The lichen appears dry and crusty during warm, sunny weather.
seasonality.fall: Still easily observed before heavy snows return to high elevations. Cool, moist conditions may make the pale background slightly more vibrant.
seasonality.winter: Often buried under snow and ice at high elevations, though it continues growing slowly beneath the white blanket, demonstrating remarkable cold tolerance.

funFact: This tough little lichen can survive being frozen solid for months at a time, then immediately resume photosynthesis when temperatures rise above freezing - essentially coming back to life after being in suspended animation all winter long.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other crusty lichens on rocks, but the distinctive dark "bloodspot" markings are usually diagnostic. If you see pale crusty lichen without the dark spots, it's probably a different species entirely.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its dramatic "bloodspot" name, this lichen is completely harmless and actually indicates clean air quality - lichens are sensitive to air pollution and won't grow in contaminated environments.
compareHints: Alpine Bloodspot Lichen is the only species in its genus found in New England, making it unique among our local lichens. Compared to other crusty rock lichens in the region, none share its distinctive combination of pale background with dark reddish-brown spots, making identification relatively straightforward once you know what to look for.
